extraction.name: PIQA: Physical Interaction: Question Answering
extraction.description: A benchmark dataset for evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding systems. The dataset consists of multiple choice questions requiring physical commonsense knowledge, with over 16,000 training QA pairs and additional held-out sets for development and testing. Questions are derived from instructables.com and focus on everyday situations with atypical solutions.
extraction.creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
extraction.publisher: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Microsoft Research AI, Carnegie Mellon University, Paul G. Allen School for Computer Science and Engineering, University of Washington
extraction.citeAs: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi. PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI 2020.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected using instructables.com as a scaffold to inspire annotators. Annotators were prompted with links to instructables and asked to extract or construct two component tasks, articulating a physical goal and how to achieve it, along with a subtle perturbation that makes the solution invalid.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data source is instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for various tasks including cooking, crafting, and home repair. Instructables were drawn from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Annotators were asked to provide semantic perturbations or alternative approaches which are otherwise syntactically and topically similar to ensure physical knowledge is targeted. They created goal-solution pairs where the goal indicates a post-condition and solutions indicate the procedure for accomplishing it.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The dataset was cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm, which performs systematic data bias reduction by discarding instances whose feature representations are collectively highly indicative of the target label. Examples with low agreement during validation were removed, particularly those requiring expert-level domain knowledge. All data was tokenized by Spacy and truncated at 150 tokens (affecting 1% of the data).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were asked to glance at instructables and construct two component tasks: 1) articulate a physical goal, 2) provide a valid solution, and 3) provide a trick (a subtle perturbation that sounds reasonable but is wrong, often due to misunderstanding of preconditions or physics). Two examples were drawn per instructable to encourage precise articulation of pre-conditions. A diff button was included in the interface to highlight where solutions differ.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. Annotators had to successfully identify well-formed goal-solution pairs (>80% accuracy) in a qualification HIT to participate in the main annotation task. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness. Users with low agreement were disqualified.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Multiple annotations per item during validation phase for agreement checking
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset was specifically designed to be adversarial to BERT and to remove annotation artifacts using AFLite. Initial unconstrained prompts led to reporting bias where annotators were drawn to prototypical solutions and common tools (e.g., forks, knives, hammers, drills) rather than considering the hundreds of other everyday objects. The instructables prompting approach was used to flatten the distribution of referenced objects.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses on physical commonsense that can be expressed in language, but due to reporting bias, many commonsense properties are rarely directly reported. Some correct examples requiring expert-level knowledge of specific domains (e.g., special woodworking terminology) were removed as they should not fall under commonsense. The dataset may not generalize to all physical reasoning scenarios. Models trained on large web crawls may eventually surpass human performance by finding large sources of in-domain data, which is not the intended purpose of the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for evaluating and studying physical commonsense understanding in natural language models. It serves as a benchmark for progress towards language representations that capture knowledge traditionally only seen or experienced. The dataset can be used as a diagnostic tool to probe the inner workings of deep pretrained language models and determine the extent of their physical knowledge. Use cases include Training, Testing, and Validation of models for physical commonsense reasoning tasks.
